blocks.text: Practice short questions for the whole of Chapter 6 (Bioenergetics), arranged by the chapter's sections, in the style of a 2-mark Board short question. Each answer is a short model answer; small numericals show the working, and a comparison is answered as a table.
Bioenergetics and ATP: the energy currency of cells

blocks.prompt: 1 Define bioenergetics. Name the two processes that help to understand its principles.
blocks.explanation: Bioenergetics is the study of how energy flows through living systems, i.e. how cells store and expend energy. Photosynthesis (an energy-capturing process) and respiration (an energy-releasing process) help to understand its principles.

book_ref.quote: It explores the processes through which cells store and expend energy

blocks.text: ATP: The Energy Currency of Cells

blocks.prompt: 2 Name the three subunits of an ATP molecule.
blocks.explanation:
1. Adenine, a nitrogen containing base
2. Ribose, a five-carbon sugar
3. Three phosphate groups

book_ref.quote: A molecule of ATP has three subunits i.e. adenine

blocks.prompt: 3 What are high-energy bonds of ATP? How much energy is released when one is broken?
blocks.explanation: The covalent bonds between two phosphate groups of ATP are high-energy bonds. Breaking one releases inorganic phosphate (Pi) and about 7.3 kcal (7,300 calories) per mole of ATP.

book_ref.quote: The covalent bonds between two phosphates are high-energy bonds

blocks.prompt: 4 Why is ATP called the energy currency of the cell?
blocks.explanation: Cells store energy from oxidation of food by combining ADP with Pi to make ATP, and break ATP when they need energy. ATP is made in energy-releasing processes and broken in energy-consuming processes, so it transfers energy between metabolic reactions like a currency.

book_ref.quote: In this way ATP transfers energy between metabolic reactions

blocks.prompt: 5 Differentiate between ADP and AMP.
blocks.explanation: ADP is formed from ATP by loss of one Pi; AMP is formed from ADP by loss of a further Pi.

book_ref.quote: When this happens, ATP becomes ADP (adenosine diphosphate) and one Pi is released

rows: Adenosine diphosphate
Adenosine monophosphate
Formed when the outer P-P bond of ATP breaks and one Pi is released
Formed in some cases when ADP is further broken down and Pi is released
ATP + H₂O → ADP + Pi + energy (7.3 kcal/mole)
ADP + H₂O → AMP + Pi + energy (7.3 kcal/mole)

blocks.prompt: 6 Water is shown on both sides of the photosynthesis equation. Is there any net yield of water?
blocks.explanation: No. Water is used as a reactant in some reactions (12H₂O) and released as a product in others (6H₂O), so it appears on both sides, but there is no net yield of water.

book_ref.quote: However, there is no net yield of water

blocks.prompt: 7 Define photosynthesis in terms of energy-poor and energy-rich compounds.
blocks.explanation: Photosynthesis is the process in which energy-poor inorganic compounds of carbon (CO₂) are reduced to energy-rich carbohydrates, using light energy absorbed and converted into chemical energy by photosynthetic pigments.

book_ref.quote: Photosynthesis is the process in which the energy-poor inorganic compounds of carbon

blocks.prompt: 8 What is compensation point?
blocks.explanation: At dawn and dusk, when light intensity is low, the rates of photosynthesis and respiration may be equal for a short time. Oxygen released by photosynthesis equals the oxygen needed for respiration, and CO₂ released by respiration equals that needed for photosynthesis. This point of no net gas exchange between leaves and atmosphere is the compensation point.

book_ref.quote: At this moment there is no net gas exchange between leaves and atmosphere

blocks.prompt: 9 Why do leaves release CO₂ in darkness but release O₂ at noon?
blocks.explanation: Photosynthesis occurs only in daytime but respiration goes on day and night. In darkness leaves only respire, so they use O₂ and release CO₂. At noon photosynthesis is fast: respiration cannot supply the CO₂ needed and more O₂ is made than respiring cells need, so there is net release of O₂ and uptake of CO₂.

book_ref.quote: Photosynthesis occurs only during day time but respiration goes on day and night

blocks.prompt: 10 Give two roles of water in photosynthesis.
blocks.explanation:
1. Water is the source of hydrogen for the reduction of CO₂ (the hydrogen reduces NADP to NADPH).
2. Oxygen released in photosynthesis comes from water, so water is an important source of atmospheric oxygen needed for aerobic respiration.

book_ref.quote: so water is an important source of atmospheric oxygen

blocks.prompt: 11 State van Niel's hypothesis. When was it confirmed?
blocks.explanation: In the 1930s C. B. van Niel hypothesized that the plant splits water as a source of hydrogen, releasing oxygen as a by-product. It was confirmed by scientists in the 1940s using the oxygen isotope ¹⁸O as a tracer.

book_ref.quote: Niel’s hypothesis was later confirmed by scientists during 1940s

blocks.prompt: 12 What is meant by 'reducing power' in photosynthesis?
blocks.explanation: In photosynthesis water is split to release hydrogen, which reduces the coenzyme NADP (nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide phosphate) to NADPH. This NADPH is the 'reducing power' used to reduce CO₂ to sugar.

book_ref.quote: The reduced coenzyme i.e., NADPH serves as the “reducing power”

blocks.prompt: 13 What are photons? What happens when a pigment molecule absorbs a photon?
blocks.explanation: Light behaves like a stream of particles called photons. A pigment molecule absorbs one photon at a time; its electrons move to a higher energy level, so the molecule becomes energy-rich or excited.

book_ref.quote: Pigment molecules absorb one photon at a time

blocks.prompt: 14 Which photons carry more energy, blue or red? What is the effect on electrons?
blocks.explanation: Short wavelength (blue) photons have higher energy than long wavelength (red) photons. More energetic photons promote electrons to higher energy levels.

book_ref.quote: More energetic photons (shorter wavelength) promote electrons to higher energy levels

blocks.prompt: 15 Name the two parts of a chlorophyll molecule and give the role of each.
blocks.explanation:
1. Hydrophilic head: a porphyrin ring of four pyrrole rings held by a central magnesium atom; it absorbs light.
2. Hydrophobic tail: a long hydrocarbon chain; it anchors the molecule in the thylakoid membrane.

book_ref.quote: A molecule of chlorophyll consists of two parts i.e., a hydrophilic head and a hydrophobic tail

blocks.prompt: 16 What are pyrrole rings? How are they held in chlorophyll?
blocks.explanation: Pyrrole rings are 5-sided nitrogen-containing compounds. Four of them make the porphyrin ring of the chlorophyll head and are held together by a magnesium atom in the centre.

book_ref.quote: which further consists of four pyrrole rings (5-sided N-containing compounds)

blocks.prompt: 17 Why do leaves look green?
blocks.explanation: Chlorophylls absorb mainly violet-blue and orange-red wavelengths. Green wavelengths are least absorbed and are transmitted or reflected, so leaves look green.

book_ref.quote: Chlorophylls absorb mainly violet-blue and orange-red wavelengths of light

blocks.prompt: 18 Write the dual role of carotenoids in photosynthesis.
blocks.explanation:
1. They capture light energy in the blue and green regions of the spectrum.
2. They protect the photosynthetic apparatus from damage by excess light.

book_ref.quote: They capture light energy in the blue and green regions of the spectrum

blocks.prompt: 19 What are accessory pigments? Give examples.
blocks.explanation: Accessory pigments are all pigments other than chlorophyll a which can gather light for photosynthesis and pass the energy towards chlorophyll a. Examples: chlorophyll b, carotenoids (carotenes and xanthophylls) and phycobilins.

book_ref.quote: which can gather light for photosynthesis

blocks.prompt: 20 Where are chlorophyll b, carotenoids and phycobilins found?
blocks.explanation: Chlorophyll b and carotenoids are found in plants, while phycobilins are found in red algae and cyanobacteria.

book_ref.quote: Chlorophyll b and carotenoids are found in plants

blocks.prompt: 21 What is an absorption spectrum? At which wavelengths do chlorophylls absorb maximum light?
blocks.explanation: A graph showing the different wavelengths absorbed by a pigment is its absorption spectrum. Chlorophylls absorb maximum blue light (430 nm) and red light (670 nm).

book_ref.quote: A graph showing different wavelengths absorbed by a pigment

blocks.prompt: 22 What does the matching of the action spectrum with the absorption spectrum show?
blocks.explanation: The action spectrum shows that blue and red light are the most effective for photosynthesis, and these are also the wavelengths best absorbed by chlorophylls. So the action spectrum of photosynthesis coincides with the absorption spectrum of photosynthetic pigments, i.e. the light absorbed by the pigments is the light that drives photosynthesis.

book_ref.quote: This means that the action spectrum of photosynthesis coincides with the absorption spectrum

blocks.prompt: 23 How is an action spectrum obtained?
blocks.explanation: A plant is illuminated with different colours of light one by one. For each colour the rate of photosynthesis is measured by measuring the oxygen emitted from the leaves. The data plotted as a graph is the action spectrum.

book_ref.quote: The effectiveness of different wavelengths of light is determined in terms of action spectrum

blocks.prompt: 24 What did Engelmann observe in Spirogyra in 1883?
blocks.explanation: T. W. Engelmann illuminated cells of a Spirogyra filament with different wavelengths. Maximum photosynthesis, and so maximum oxygen emission, occurred in the cells that received blue and red light. This was the first action spectrum.

book_ref.quote: When the cells of a filament of Spirogyra were illuminated with different wavelengths of light

blocks.prompt: 25 How efficiently do plants convert solar energy into chemical energy?
blocks.explanation: Plants convert only about 1-2% of the solar energy they receive into chemical energy. Despite this low efficiency it is enough to sustain almost all life on Earth.

book_ref.quote: Despite this seemingly low efficiency, this conversion is enough to sustain almost all life on Earth

blocks.prompt: 26 How does CO₂ reach the mesophyll cells of a leaf?
blocks.explanation: CO₂ enters the leaves through stomata (found in large numbers in leaves) and dissolves in the water absorbed by the cell walls of mesophyll cells. Its entry depends on the opening of stomata.

book_ref.quote: Carbon dioxide enters the leaves through stomata and gets dissolved in water

blocks.prompt: 27 Compare the carbon sources of aquatic and land photosynthetic organisms.
blocks.explanation: Aquatic organisms use dissolved carbon sources; land organisms use atmospheric CO₂.

book_ref.quote: Land photosynthetic organisms use atmospheric CO₂ as carbon source

rows: Use dissolved CO₂
Use atmospheric CO₂
Also use bicarbonates and soluble carbonates
CO₂ enters the leaves through stomata

blocks.prompt: 28 On which organisms was van Niel's hypothesis based?
blocks.explanation: It was based on investigations on photosynthetic bacteria that make carbohydrate from carbon dioxide but do not release oxygen.

book_ref.quote: Niel’s hypothesis was based on the investigations on photosynthetic bacteria

blocks.prompt: 29 Differentiate between antenna complex and reaction centre of a photosystem.
blocks.explanation: The antenna complex gathers light; the reaction centre passes high-energy electrons on.

book_ref.quote: Antenna complex has many pigment molecules which capture light energy

rows: Light-gathering part of the photosystem
Central part of the photosystem
Has many pigment molecules
Has one or more molecules of chlorophyll a
Captures light and passes excitation energy to the reaction centre
Passes high-energy electrons to a primary electron acceptor

blocks.prompt: 30 Differentiate between PS-I and PS-II on the basis of their reaction centres.
blocks.explanation: PS-I has P700 and PS-II has P680 chlorophyll a in the reaction centre.

book_ref.quote: The reaction centre of PS-II has P680 chlorophyll-a, which absorbs best the light of 680 nm

rows: Reaction centre has P700 chlorophyll a
Reaction centre has P680 chlorophyll a
Absorbs maximum light of 700 nm
Absorbs best the light of 680 nm
Discovered first, so named I
Discovered second, so named II

blocks.prompt: 31 Name the three key events of the light-dependent reactions.
blocks.explanation:
1. Absorption of light energy by photosynthetic pigments
2. Excitation of electrons by that energy
3. Formation of ATP and NADPH

book_ref.quote: the absorption of light energy by photosynthetic pigments, (2) the excitation of electrons by that energy

blocks.prompt: 32 Name the reducing and assimilating powers formed in the light-dependent reactions. Where are they used?
blocks.explanation: Light energy is converted into chemical energy in the form of reducing and assimilating powers, NADPH and ATP. The light-independent reactions use them to reduce CO₂ and store chemical energy as C-H bond energy.

book_ref.quote: which is in the form of reducing and assimilating powers i.e., NADPH and ATP

blocks.prompt: 33 What is photolysis? Write its products.
blocks.explanation: Photolysis is the water-splitting step of photosynthesis. Water reacts with oxidized chlorophyll of PS-II and breaks into two hydrogen ions, an oxygen atom (which joins another to form O₂) and two electrons. The electrons fill the 'hole' in P680.

book_ref.quote: These two electrons fill the “hole” in P680 chlorophyll

blocks.prompt: 34 How is NADPH formed in the light-dependent reactions?
blocks.explanation: The primary electron acceptor of PS-I passes photoexcited electrons to ferredoxin (FD). The enzyme NADP reductase transfers them from FD to NADP⁺. NADP⁺ gets two electrons and an H⁺ ion and is reduced to NADPH, storing the high-energy electrons.

book_ref.quote: When NADP⁺ gets two electrons and an H⁺ ion, it is reduced to NADPH

blocks.prompt: 35 What is Z-scheme?
blocks.explanation: In non-cyclic photophosphorylation electrons take a zigzag path through PS-II, PS-I and the electron transport chains. This zigzag path is called the Z-scheme.

book_ref.quote: electron transport chains, is called Z-scheme

blocks.prompt: 36 Compare non-cyclic and cyclic photophosphorylation.
blocks.explanation: Non-cyclic flow uses both photosystems and makes ATP, NADPH and O₂; cyclic flow uses PS-I only and makes ATP only.

book_ref.quote: It is the usual way of the production of ATPs during light-dependent reactions

rows: Usual way of making ATP in light-dependent reactions
Happens when the Calvin cycle slows down and NADPH accumulates
Both PS-I and PS-II take part
Uses PS-I but not PS-II
Electrons end in NADPH
Electrons cycle back to P700 chlorophyll
Produces ATP, NADPH and O₂
Produces ATP only; no NADPH and no O₂

blocks.prompt: 37 How is the H⁺ gradient built up in the thylakoid?
blocks.explanation: Electrons lose energy as they pass from carrier to carrier in the electron transport chain. This energy is spent on active transport of H⁺ ions from the stroma into the lumen, so many H⁺ ions collect in the lumen. This H⁺ gradient has potential energy.

book_ref.quote: This H⁺ ion gradient in lumen has potential energy

blocks.prompt: 38 What is the role of ATP synthase in the chloroplast?
blocks.explanation: H⁺ ions diffuse back from the lumen to the stroma through ATP synthase, a protein of the thylakoid membrane. The enzyme uses the energy of this H⁺ flow to bond ADP with inorganic phosphate (Pi), forming ATP.

book_ref.quote: This enzyme uses the energy yielded from the flow of H⁺ ions to make a bond between ADP and inorganic phosphate

blocks.prompt: 39 What do the light-independent reactions take from CO₂, ATP and NADPH?
blocks.explanation: They take carbon from CO₂, energy from ATP and hydrogen ions from NADPH to construct energy-rich sugar molecules in the stroma.

book_ref.quote: These reactions use carbon from CO₂, energy from ATP, and hydrogen ions from NADPH

blocks.prompt: 40 Why are the dark reactions called the Calvin cycle?
blocks.explanation: Their details were discovered by Melvin Calvin and his colleagues at the University of California, so they are called the Calvin cycle. Calvin received the Nobel Prize in 1961 for this work.

book_ref.quote: That is why, the dark reactions are also called the Calvin cycle

blocks.prompt: 41 Name the three phases of the Calvin cycle.
blocks.explanation:
1. Carbon fixation
2. Reduction
3. Regeneration of RuBP

book_ref.quote: The Calvin cycle is divided into the following phases

blocks.prompt: 42 What is formed when rubisco combines three CO₂ with three RuBP?
blocks.explanation: Six molecules of a three-carbon compound, 3-phosphoglyceric acid (3-PGA) or 3-phosphoglycerate, are formed. Because this first product has three carbons, the Calvin cycle is called the C-3 pathway.

book_ref.quote: It results in the formation of six molecules of a three–carbon compound called 3–phosphoglyceric acid

blocks.prompt: 43 What happens to the G3P that leaves the Calvin cycle?
blocks.explanation: Of six G3P produced, one leaves the cycle. It combines with another G3P to make glucose, which may then be converted to other carbohydrates.

book_ref.quote: It combines with another G3P and makes glucose

blocks.prompt: 44 How is RuBP regenerated in the Calvin cycle?
blocks.explanation: Through a series of reactions five G3P are converted into three ribulose phosphate (RuP). One phosphate group is added to each RuP, using three ATPs of the light reactions, to make three RuBP, which receive CO₂ again.

book_ref.quote: One phosphate group is added to each RuP to make three molecules of RuBP by using three ATPs

blocks.prompt: 45 Define cellular respiration and write its summary equation.
blocks.explanation:
Cellular respiration is the universal process by which organisms break down complex carbon-containing compounds (e.g. glucose) to get usable energy, by step-by-step oxidation of food in the cells.
C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂ → 6CO₂ + 6H₂O + Energy

book_ref.quote: Cellular respiration is the universal process by which organisms break down complex carbon containing compounds

blocks.prompt: 46 Differentiate between external respiration and cellular respiration.
blocks.explanation: External respiration is gas exchange with the environment; cellular respiration is oxidation of food inside cells.

book_ref.quote: Cellular respiration is the process by which energy is made available to cells

rows: Also called breathing
Occurs inside the cells
Exchange of CO₂ and O₂ between the organism and its environment
Step-by-step oxidation of food in the cells that makes energy available

blocks.prompt: 47 Name the two main types of cellular respiration. Which step is common to both?
blocks.explanation:
1. Anaerobic respiration (fermentation), in the absence of oxygen
2. Aerobic respiration, in the presence of oxygen
In the first step of both, glucose splits into two pyruvic acid (C₃H₄O₃) by glycolysis.

book_ref.quote: Anaerobic respiration (fermentation) takes place in the absence of oxygen

blocks.prompt: 48 Why does anaerobic respiration yield little energy?
blocks.explanation: In anaerobic respiration glucose is not completely oxidized. One glucose yields only two ATPs, about 2% of the energy present in glucose (equivalent to 14.6 kcal).

book_ref.quote: In anaerobic respiration, glucose is not completely oxidized

blocks.prompt: 49 Differentiate between alcoholic fermentation and lactic acid fermentation.
blocks.explanation: Alcoholic fermentation gives ethyl alcohol and CO₂; lactic acid fermentation gives lactic acid only.

book_ref.quote: Lactic acid fermentation releases no carbon dioxide

rows: Pyruvic acid forms ethyl alcohol (C₂H₅OH) and CO₂
Pyruvic acid forms lactic acid (C₃H₆O₃); no CO₂ is released
2(C₃H₄O₃) + 4H → 2(C₂H₅OH) + 2CO₂
2(C₃H₄O₃) + 4H → 2(C₃H₆O₃)
Occurs in some bacteria and in yeast
Occurs in muscle cells of humans and other animals, and many bacteria

blocks.prompt: 50 Why does lactic acid form in human muscles?
blocks.explanation: During extreme physical activity oxygen cannot be transported to the muscle cells as rapidly as it is needed. The cells then carry out lactic acid fermentation, converting pyruvic acid into lactic acid.

book_ref.quote: It happens during extreme physical activities, when oxygen cannot be transported to the cells

blocks.prompt: 51 Name the four stages of aerobic respiration with their sites.
blocks.explanation:
1. Glycolysis: cytosol
2. Pyruvic acid oxidation: mitochondria
3. Krebs cycle (citric acid cycle): mitochondria
4. Electron transport chain and chemiosmosis: mitochondria (inner membrane)

book_ref.quote: Cellular respiration is a continuous process, but for study purposes we can divide it into four main stages

blocks.prompt: 52 Name the two phases of glycolysis and state the main event of each.
blocks.explanation:
1. Preparatory phase: energy (2 ATP) is spent and glucose is broken into two G3P.
2. Oxidative phase: hydrogen is removed from G3P and the released energy is packed as ATP.

book_ref.quote: Glucose 6-phosphate is converted into its isomer called fructose 6-phosphate

blocks.prompt: 53 Besides enzymes, which substances are essential for glycolysis? Where are its enzymes found?
blocks.explanation: Besides enzymes, ATP and the coenzyme NAD⁺ (nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide) are essential. All enzymes of glycolysis are found dissolved in the cytosol.

book_ref.quote: In addition to the enzymes, ATP and coenzyme NAD⁺ (nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide) are also essential

blocks.prompt: 54 What is gluconeogenesis?
blocks.explanation: Pyruvic acid can be turned back into glucose by reversing glycolysis. This is called gluconeogenesis.

book_ref.quote: Pyruvic acid can also be turned back into glucose by reversing glycolysis

blocks.prompt: 55 How does glucose enter cells?
blocks.explanation: Glucose enters cells from the tissue fluid by passive transport using a specific glucose carrier. This carrier can be controlled (gated) by hormones such as insulin.

book_ref.quote: This carrier can be controlled (gated) by hormones such as insulin

blocks.prompt: 56 What is acetyl-CoA? How is it formed?
blocks.explanation: Acetyl-CoA is the product of pyruvic acid oxidation that enters the Krebs cycle. CO₂ is removed from pyruvic acid to form acetaldehyde, which is oxidized (NAD⁺ → NADH) to an acetyl group; the acetyl group combines with coenzyme A to form acetyl-CoA.

book_ref.quote: Acetyl group combines with coenzyme-A (CoA) to form acetyl-CoA

blocks.prompt: 57 Why is it not correct to say that respiration turns oxygen into carbon dioxide?
blocks.explanation: Carbon dioxide is released (in pyruvic acid oxidation and the Krebs cycle) before oxygen is involved. Oxygen is used only at the end of the electron transport chain, where it forms water. So respiration turns glucose into CO₂ and oxygen into water.

book_ref.quote: It is more correct to say that respiration turns glucose into carbon dioxide, and oxygen into water

blocks.prompt: 58 What is oxidative decarboxylation? Give one example from the Krebs cycle.
blocks.explanation: In oxidative decarboxylation a molecule is decarboxylated (a CO₂ is released) and oxidized (an NAD⁺ is reduced to NADH). Example: citric acid (6-C) changes to alpha-ketoglutaric acid (5-C).

book_ref.quote: Citric acid undergoes an oxidative decarboxylation reaction

blocks.prompt: 59 At which step of the Krebs cycle is ATP made directly?
blocks.explanation: The bond between succinic acid and CoA in succinyl CoA is a high-energy linkage. When succinyl CoA splits into CoA and succinic acid, the energy released is used to make one ATP.

book_ref.quote: The bond between succinic acid and CoA is a high-energy linkage

blocks.prompt: 60 Why is the Krebs cycle called a cycle?
blocks.explanation: Its first step uses oxaloacetic acid to combine with the acetyl group, and its last step (oxidation of malic acid) regenerates oxaloacetic acid, which is free to bind another acetyl CoA. So the series of reactions repeats as a cycle.

book_ref.quote: This completes the cycle and oxaloacetic acid is now free to bind another molecule of acetyl CoA

blocks.prompt: 61 Write the sequence of electron carriers in the respiratory electron transport chain.
blocks.explanation: NADH (or FADH₂) → coenzyme Q → cytochrome b → cytochrome c → cytochrome a complex → oxygen

book_ref.quote: The reduced CoQ transports electrons to cytochrome ‘b’

blocks.prompt: 62 How is water formed at the end of the respiratory electron transport chain?
blocks.explanation: Cytochrome a complex passes electrons to an oxygen atom at the bottom end of the chain. The oxygen atom takes two electrons and two hydrogen ions and forms water.

book_ref.quote: At the end, the two hydrogen ions are taken by the oxygen atom which has also taken two electrons to form water

blocks.prompt: 63 What is phosphorylation? Name the two ways by which a cell does it.
blocks.explanation:
Phosphorylation is adding a phosphate group to ADP to generate ATP. A cell does it by:
1. Chemiosmotic phosphorylation (chemiosmosis)
2. Substrate-level phosphorylation

book_ref.quote: Cells generate ATP by phosphorylation i.e. adding a phosphate group to ADP

blocks.prompt: 64 How many ATP are obtained from one NADH of the Krebs cycle, one NADH of glycolysis and one FADH₂?
blocks.explanation:
1. NADH of the Krebs cycle: 3 ATP
2. NADH of glycolysis: 2 ATP (one ATP is spent to carry it across the mitochondrial membrane)
3. FADH₂: 2 ATP

book_ref.quote: Each FADH₂ molecule leads to the production of two ATP molecules

blocks.prompt: 65 Aerobic oxidation is said to be 18 times more efficient than anaerobic. Explain.
blocks.explanation: Aerobic oxidation of one glucose gives a net profit of 36 ATP, while anaerobic oxidation (glycolysis only) gives only 2 ATP. 36 ÷ 2 = 18, so aerobic oxidation is 18 times more efficient.

book_ref.quote: While during the glycolysis of anaerobic oxidation only 2 ATP molecules are generated

blocks.prompt: 66 Name the food substances other than glucose that we consume as respiratory fuel.
blocks.explanation: Free glucose is not common in our diet. We consume sucrose and other disaccharides, starch, fats and proteins. Proteins are used only after digestion to amino acids, and fats after hydrolysis into glycerol and fatty acids.

book_ref.quote: Free glucose molecules are not common in our diet

blocks.prompt: 67 What is photorespiration? How does it differ from aerobic respiration in its product?
blocks.explanation: Photorespiration is the respiratory activity of green cells in the presence of light that releases CO₂. Like aerobic respiration it needs oxygen and produces CO₂ and H₂O, but no ATP is produced.

book_ref.quote: The respiratory activity that occurs in green cells in the presence of light resulting in release of carbon dioxide

blocks.prompt: 68 Under what condition does rubisco add O₂ instead of CO₂ to RuBP?
blocks.explanation: When the relative concentration of CO₂ decreases and there is more oxygen in leaf cells, rubisco adds O₂ to RuBP. RuBP then breaks into one phosphoglycerate and one phosphoglycolate.

book_ref.quote: However, when the relative concentration of CO₂ decreases and there is more oxygen in leaf cells

blocks.prompt: 69 Name the three organelles involved in photorespiration.
blocks.explanation:
1. Chloroplast: phosphoglycolate forms and changes to glycolate; glycerate returns as phosphoglycerate.
2. Peroxisome: glycolate to glyoxylate (with H₂O₂) and glycine; serine to glycerate.
3. Mitochondrion: two glycine form one serine.

book_ref.quote: Phosphoglycolate is converted into glycolate, which moves from chloroplast to peroxisome

blocks.prompt: 70 What are C-3 plants? How does photorespiration affect them?
blocks.explanation: Plants that fix carbon only by the Calvin cycle are C-3 plants. When photorespiration occurs in them they lose 25% to 50% of their fixed carbon, which reduces their yields.

book_ref.quote: Plants that use Calvin cycle to fix carbon are called C-3 plants

blocks.prompt: 71 Why was there little or no photorespiration when photosynthesis first evolved?
blocks.explanation: At that time there was little oxygen in the atmosphere, so O₂ did not compete with CO₂ for rubisco. After millions of years free O₂ accumulated and competition for the same active site of rubisco started, causing photorespiration.

book_ref.quote: When photosynthesis first evolved, there was little oxygen in the atmosphere

blocks.text: Adaptations to the problems of Photorespiration

blocks.prompt: 72 Write two features of the leaves of C-4 plants.
blocks.explanation:
1. Mesophyll cells have less air spaces.
2. Enzymes of the Calvin cycle are deposited mostly in specialized bundle-sheath cells, which are impermeable to CO₂.

book_ref.quote: In their leaves, the mesophyll cells have less air spaces

blocks.prompt: 73 C-4 photosynthesis costs almost double energy. Why is it still useful in hot climates?
blocks.explanation: In hot climates photorespiration would otherwise remove more than half of the fixed carbon. C-4 plants keep CO₂ concentrated in bundle-sheath cells, so they run the Calvin cycle instead of photorespiration. Hence, despite the cost, it is the best compromise available.

book_ref.quote: However, in hot climates, in which photorespiration would otherwise remove more than half of the carbon fixed

blocks.prompt: 74 How do CAM plants reduce photorespiration?
blocks.explanation: Their stomata open at night and close during the day. Closing stomata in the day prevents water loss and removal of CO₂, so the high CO₂ concentration reduces photorespiration. The CO₂ for making sugar comes from organic molecules made the night before.

book_ref.quote: Closing stomata during the day prevents water loss and removal of CO₂

blocks.prompt: 75 Give two examples of CAM plants. Which pathways do they use?
blocks.explanation: Examples: cacti and pineapples (succulent plants of hot climates). Like C-4 plants, they use both C-4 and C-3 pathways.

book_ref.quote: Like C-4 plants, these plants use both C-4 and C-3 pathways
